strengths: The paper identifies an important failure mode: a predictor may learn an invariant cue that is unavailable after deployment. The SIL framing usefully emphasizes redundancy among invariant cues rather than only suppressing spurious correlations.
ASGDRO is simple and model-agnostic, combining group-robust weighting with adaptive sharpness optimization. The manuscript provides pseudocode, substantial hyperparameter details, and a code link.

The empirical scope is broad. ASGDRO improves GDRO on H-CMNIST TestBed 2 (69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03), is competitive on four subpopulation-shift datasets, and raises the training-domain DomainBed average of DPLCLIP from 72.6 to 74.0.

H-CMNIST, Grad-CAM visualizations, and per-group Hessian measurements attempt to examine mechanism rather than reporting benchmark accuracy alone. The motivation and overall experimental narrative are generally clear.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. With Z=(1,…,1), θλ=λ, and ∑iλi=1, the MSE prediction, risk, gradient −(Y−1)1, and exact Euclidean parameter-robust loss are all independent of λ. The proof introduces −λ⊙∇R without justification, so the claimed preference for λ=(1/p,…,1/p) does not follow. This undermines the main theoretical support for balanced invariant-feature use.

The central bridge from parameter-space flatness to feature diversity is not established. Linear interpolation between singleton-feature mechanisms is asserted to represent arbitrary feature subsets, which is generally invalid for nonlinear networks and interacting features. Parameter perturbations also need not correspond to input-feature removal or occlusion. Proposition 1 only gives a first-order gradient-norm approximation; a small gradient occurs at both sharp and flat stationary points and does not prove convergence to a common flat minimum. Appendix A.5 similarly assumes, without support, that high-loss activated neurons encode spurious rather than invariant information.

The SIL definition is underspecified and unusually strong. Its optimization ranges over E, apparently including unseen environments; the masking/intervention represented by h(ẐI) is undefined; and the maximum over all subsets includes the empty set unless silently excluded. Appendix A.2 assumes additional features cannot hurt and then reduces the objective to singleton subsets, effectively requiring every individual invariant feature to be sufficient. No theorem connects this definition to robustness under test-time feature absence.

Evidence for the defining SIL claim is largely confined to a two-cue synthetic dataset. Standard subpopulation, WILDS, and DomainBed accuracies do not identify multiple invariant cues or test controlled removal of such cues. Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and do not establish which features causally determine predictions, while lower Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate at most the optimized sharpness property, not invariant-feature diversity. H-CMNIST uses only three seeds and its principal TestBed 2 result has high variability.

The implemented method differs materially from the analyzed objective: almost all experiments use one perturbation computed from aggregate empirical risk rather than the environment-specific perturbations in Eq. 3 and Algorithm 1, without an approximation analysis or controlled ablation. Comparisons also omit a non-adaptive SAM-plus-GDRO variant that would isolate the proposed components.

Some experimental reporting is insufficiently consistent for reproduction. WILDS lacks complete architecture, training, model-selection, and group-construction details, and several baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun under the reported search. Moreover, RxRx1 ASGDRO is 32.2±0.2 in Table 3 but 30.5±0.1 in Figure 7. These issues are secondary to the theoretical problems but weaken confidence in the broad empirical claims. Overall, the useful framing and promising results constitute worthwhile merit, but the invalid central theorem and missing evidence for the claimed mechanism make the current balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful robustness failure: a model may learn an invariant cue yet fail when that particular cue is missing. The SIL framing and bird example communicate this motivation clearly.
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically implementable, combining group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware training.
The controlled H-CMNIST experiment provides promising evidence: ASGDRO reaches 69.17±6.19 shape-only accuracy versus 61.44±1.03 for GDRO, despite color being the easier invariant cue.

The evaluation is broad. ASGDRO is competitive on four subpopulation-shift datasets, multiple WILDS tasks, and five DomainBed datasets; for example, DPLCLIP+ASGDRO improves the DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0.
The manuscript provides pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, architectures, seed counts, hardware information, error bars for many results, and a code link, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central formalization is not technically sound. Joint invariance of Z^I does not imply that every subset is invariant or individually predictive, yet SIL requires robustness over all subsets. The definition apparently includes the empty subset and optimizes over all environments, including unavailable test environments. The appendix's monotonicity assumption does not resolve these issues or justify representing subset mechanisms through parameter interpolation.

Theorem 1 appears false under its own assumptions. With Z=(1,...,1) and sum_i lambda_i=1, the linear prediction and MSE are independent of lambda; the exact worst-case loss over an L2 parameter ball is likewise independent of lambda. The proof introduces lambda elementwise-multiplied by the gradient without justification, so the claimed uniform solution lambda_i=1/p does not follow. This invalidates the main theoretical support for learning balanced invariant mechanisms.

The remaining common-flat-minimum argument is also insufficient: linear mode connectivity does not imply low loss throughout a Euclidean ball, small gradient norm at a stationary point does not distinguish sharp from flat minima, and the appendix assumes without evidence that high-risk active neurons encode spurious features.

The experiments use one perturbation computed from average risk, whereas the stated objective and analysis use a separately maximized perturbation for every environment. Consequently, the theory does not analyze the method actually evaluated.

Only synthetic H-CMNIST directly tests survival after removing an invariant cue, and its key results have substantial variance over just three seeds. Standard benchmark accuracy, qualitative Grad-CAM examples, and scale-dependent Hessian eigenvalues do not establish that gains arise from diverse invariant features rather than generic sharpness regularization.

Essential ablations are missing, including standard SAM-GDRO versus adaptive normalization, environment-specific versus shared perturbations, and matched-cost comparisons. Several baselines are imported from other studies, and many improvements are modest relative to reported variability. Minor grammar and terminology problems are presentation refinements; these scientific gaps, particularly the invalid theorem, determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper identifies an important failure mode: a model can rely on only one invariant cue and fail when that cue is occluded, cropped, or otherwise unavailable. The proposed Sufficient Invariant Learning framing is intuitive and potentially useful.

ASGDRO is a simple, model-agnostic combination of adaptive sharpness-aware optimization and group reweighting. It produces promising results, including 69.17% versus GDRO's 61.44% on the shape-only H-CMNIST test, 91.4% versus 90.6% Waterbirds worst-group accuracy, and a 74.0 versus 72.9 DomainBed average when combined with DPLCLIP.

The evaluation is broad, covering a purpose-built synthetic benchmark, several subpopulation-shift datasets, WILDS, and DomainBed. Grad-CAM examples and Hessian measurements provide useful diagnostic evidence beyond accuracy alone.

The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear. It supplies pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, three-seed error bars for many experiments, hardware information, and a public code link, while acknowledging the extra training pass and lack of a real-world SIL benchmark.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Definition 1 only states invariance of E[Y|Z_I] for the joint feature set, but the paper then asserts that the condition holds for every subset and that a classifier using any such subset can be optimal. This does not follow: after marginalizing omitted features, E[Y|Z_hat] may vary across environments, and individual features need not even be predictive. Definition 3 also maximizes over all subsets, apparently including the empty set, without defining how a fixed classifier consumes a missing subset. Appendix A.2 resolves this only by introducing the strong, unformalized assumption that every observed invariant feature individually yields small loss.

Material technical issue: Theorem 1 is incorrect under its own stated setup. With Z=(1,...,1) and theta_lambda a convex combination of one-hot classifiers, sum(theta_lambda)=1, so both the prediction and the exact L2-robust squared loss are independent of lambda; the latter is proportional to (|Y-1|+rho*sqrt(p))^2. It therefore cannot uniquely select uniform lambda. The proof introduces a lambda-wise multiplication of the gradient without derivation. Earlier, the manuscript also equates the maximum risk over finitely many invariant mechanisms with the maximum over an enclosing parameter ball, whereas containment yields only an inequality.

The claimed bridge from parameter-space flatness to semantic feature diversity is not established. Proposition 1 is just a first-order SAM approximation involving gradient norm; every differentiable stationary point has zero gradient regardless of Hessian sharpness. Moreover, arbitrary local weight perturbations are not equivalent to removing individual input features. The lower Hessian eigenvalues and selected Grad-CAM visualizations show correlation, not that common flatness causes the use of multiple invariant cues.

The theory does not cover the implemented method. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 construct a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, but all substantive experiments instead use one perturbation computed from pooled empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel in that pooled direction, so this is not an approximation to each environment's inner maximization, and none of the stated SIL conclusions applies to the reported implementation.

Direct evidence for the central SIL claim is limited to synthetic H-CMNIST. Its decisive shape-only result uses only three seeds and has high variability for ASGDRO (69.17+/-6.19). The real-image benchmarks do not explicitly remove or occlude distinct invariant cues, so their accuracy gains could reflect ordinary SAM/group-DRO regularization rather than greater cue diversity. Grad-CAM is qualitative and no quantitative feature-masking, attribution-diversity, or real-world missing-cue evaluation is provided.

The algorithmic novelty is modest because ASGDRO largely combines ASAM-style perturbations with standard GDRO exponential group weighting. Essential ablations are absent, including adaptive versus ordinary SAM, pooled versus per-environment perturbations, and the separate contribution of normalization and group weighting.

Experimental control and reproducibility remain incomplete. Many baselines in Tables 2 and 3 are imported from other papers rather than rerun under matched tuning; H-CMNIST sample counts and model-selection details are omitted; and the efficiency and sensitivity studies promised in Section 4.3 do not appear in the appendix. The prose also overstates Table 2 by claiming best average and worst-group performance on all but CivilComments, although ASAM has higher Waterbirds average accuracy and ERM has higher CelebA average accuracy. These issues compound the central theoretical flaws, so the empirical promise is not yet sufficient for acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and practically important failure mode: an invariant predictor may depend on only one stable cue and fail when that cue is occluded or missing. The motivating example and SIL framing are intuitive and relevant to robust vision.

ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and readily composable with existing training methods. Its practical common-perturbation variant avoids scaling the number of perturbation computations with the number of environments.

The evaluation is broad and shows a generally favorable empirical pattern. Examples include 69.17±6.19 versus GDRO's 61.44±1.03 on the H-CMNIST shape-only test, 91.4% versus 90.6% Waterbirds worst-group accuracy, and 74.0 versus 72.9 average DomainBed accuracy when combined with DPLCLIP.

H-CMNIST provides a useful controlled test in which one invariant cue can be removed. The subpopulation, WILDS, and DomainBed experiments additionally suggest that the optimizer may be practically useful beyond this synthetic setting.
The motivation and algorithm are mostly understandable, and the appendix supplies hyperparameter ranges and seed counts for several experiments, error bars, and a code link.
weaknesses: Material: Theorem 1 is false under its stated assumptions. For p=2, Z=(1,1), Y=1, and θλ=(λ,1−λ), every λ has zero risk and the exact inner objective is max_{||ε||≤ρ} 0.5(ε1+ε2)^2=ρ², independent of λ; its first-order approximation is also zero. Thus ASGDRO does not prefer λ=(1/2,1/2) in this valid instance. The proof introduces −λ⊙∇R without derivation and uses an unsupported norm factorization, so the principal claim that sharpness enforces balanced invariant-feature use is not established.

Material: The SIL formulation relies on unjustified assumptions. Invariance conditional on the full feature set does not imply invariance or predictiveness for every subset. As written, the maximum also includes the empty subset, the behavior of h when variables are absent is undefined, and optimization over E uses environments unavailable during training. The claim that arbitrary subset mechanisms can, without loss of generality, be represented by parameter interpolation of singleton mechanisms is generally false for nonlinear networks and interacting features.

Material: The analyzed objective and the evaluated algorithm differ. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separate worst-case perturbation for each environment, whereas nearly all experiments use one perturbation obtained from average empirical risk. No equivalence or guarantee is given for this practical variant; in particular, opposing environment gradients can cancel in the averaged perturbation.

Material: Proposition 1 is only a first-order Taylor approximation and does not prove flatness—every differentiable local minimum has zero gradient regardless of Hessian sharpness. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, without justification, that highly activated neurons in a high-loss group encode spurious rather than useful invariant information. These arguments do not establish either common flat minima or removal of spurious features.

Material: Direct evidence for SIL is confined to synthetic H-CMNIST, evaluated with only three seeds and substantial variability. The standard distribution-shift benchmarks do not remove identified invariant cues or quantify feature diversity. Lower Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate relative flatness at most, while selected Grad-CAM examples are subjective and cannot show that multiple independent invariant mechanisms were learned.

Material: ASGDRO is largely a direct composition of adaptive SAM and GDRO, yet there is no matched comparison against non-adaptive SAM+GDRO, the theoretical per-environment-perturbation version, or the closest cited sharpness-aware domain-generalization methods. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate which component causes the gains, and the algorithmic originality is limited if the SIL theory is unsupported.

Reproducibility and presentation: Several competitors are imported from other papers despite potentially different tuning budgets, while ASGDRO receives sizeable searches over radius, robust step size, and group adjustment. WILDS training, backbone, and model-selection details are largely absent. The manuscript promises sensitivity and efficiency analyses but reports neither, beyond acknowledging two forward/backward passes. These issues are secondary to the theoretical defects but weaken the strength of the empirical comparisons.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful robustness problem: a predictor can rely on one invariant cue that later becomes unobserved. H-CMNIST provides a useful controlled test by removing the easy color cue while retaining digit shape.
ASGDRO is simple and potentially useful: it combines worst-group optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware perturbations and can be applied to different architectures and tasks.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and generally favorable. For example, ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44% to 69.17%, Waterbirds worst-group accuracy from 90.6% to 91.4%, and CelebA worst-group accuracy from 87.2% to 91.0%. DPLCLIP+ASGDRO also averages 74.0 on DomainBed versus 72.6 for DPLCLIP and 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO under training-domain model selection.

The manuscript is readable, includes pseudocode, reports many hyperparameter ranges and three-seed error bars, acknowledges the approximately doubled SAM-style training cost, and provides a code URL. Minor wording and typographical issues do not determine the score.
weaknesses: The central Theorem 1 is incorrect as stated. Under its assumptions, Z=(1,...,1) and theta_lambda is a convex combination of one-hot classifiers, so Z theta_lambda=1 for every lambda. With MSE and an ordinary L2 perturbation, the exact worst-case loss is independent of lambda—for y=1 it equals p*rho^2/2—so the uniform lambda is not the unique minimizer. The proof introduces a lambda-weighted gradient without deriving it, apparently importing adaptive scaling that is absent from the theorem's objective. Consequently, the theorem does not establish that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms.

Proposition 1 also does not justify the claimed common flat minimum: every differentiable stationary point has zero gradient, including arbitrarily sharp minima, so the first-order gradient-norm expression cannot distinguish sharpness at a minimum. The appendix's spurious-feature argument additionally assumes without proof that high-loss activated neurons encode spurious information and that the update deactivates them.

There is a consequential mismatch between the analyzed objective and the evaluated algorithm. The theory uses a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, whereas all substantive experiments use one perturbation computed from aggregate empirical risk. Group gradients can cancel in that aggregate, so this implementation need not control each group's sharpness. Adaptive parameter scaling is likewise used in implementation but omitted from the main theoretical objective.

The SIL formulation is not well posed generally. It optimizes over all environments, including unavailable test environments; maximizes over all feature subsets without excluding the empty subset; and does not define how one fixed classifier consumes varying subsets. The reduction to singleton features assumes each invariant cue is individually sufficient and that adding cues never hurts. The appendix's observation-probability argument does not prove the claimed equivalence between feature subsets and parameter interpolation, especially for nonlinear networks.

Only H-CMNIST directly tests missing invariant cues, and its key ASGDRO result has high variability over just three seeds (69.17±6.19). Standard subpopulation, WILDS, and DomainBed results demonstrate useful OOD performance but cannot show that improvements arise from learning more invariant features rather than ordinary sharpness regularization. Selected Grad-CAM examples do not quantify feature diversity, while lower Hessian eigenvalues provide correlation rather than a causal connection to SIL.

The algorithmic novelty is limited because the practical method is largely adaptive SAM combined with GDRO. Missing ablations—per-environment versus shared perturbations, adaptive versus ordinary perturbations, sensitivity to rho, runtime, and feature-masking tests—make the proposed mechanism difficult to isolate. Several comparisons reuse results from other papers, and the original DomainBed experiment lacks error bars and complete search details. These substantive correctness and validation gaps outweigh the promising empirical results, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The paper identifies an intuitive and practically important failure mode: a predictor may learn an invariant feature that is absent or occluded at test time, motivating redundancy across invariant cues.

H-CMNIST is a useful controlled diagnostic. ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy from 61.44±1.03 for GDRO to 69.17±6.19, providing direct—though synthetic—evidence that it can retain a harder invariant cue.

The empirical study is broad, covering subpopulation shifts, WILDS, and DomainBed with ResNet, DistilBERT, and CLIP-based models. ASGDRO generally improves over GDRO, including 91.4% versus 90.6% worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds and 74.0 versus 72.9 average DomainBed accuracy with DPLCLIP.
The method is simple and model-agnostic, and the manuscript provides error bars, hyperparameter ranges, implementation pseudocode, and a code link.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is not established. In Appendix A.4, for the stated MSE risk R(theta)=1/2|Y-sum_i theta_i|^2, the gradient components are identical and, under sum_i lambda_i=1, do not acquire the inserted factor lambda. The step replacing the gradient by -lambda elementwise-multiplied with the gradient is unjustified for the stated additive L2 perturbation. Consequently, the ||lambda|| term and the conclusion that ASGDRO selects uniform use of invariant mechanisms do not follow. A parameter-weighted ASAM constraint might support a related argument, but that is not the theorem that is stated or proved.

The SIL formulation relies on strong unstated assumptions. Conditional invariance of the joint feature set does not imply that every singleton feature is individually predictive or supports an optimal classifier. Definition 3 also maximizes over all subsets, apparently including the empty set, while Appendix A.2 reduces this to singletons by assuming that any observed invariant feature gives small loss and that adding features never hurts. These assumptions make the claimed guarantee substantially narrower than presented.

There is a consequential mismatch between analysis and implementation: Eq. (3), Algorithm 1, and the theoretical discussion use a separate adversarial perturbation for each environment, whereas nearly all experiments use one perturbation computed from aggregate empirical risk. Thus the theory does not directly characterize the evaluated algorithm.

Only H-CMNIST directly tests removal of an invariant cue. Standard OOD and worst-group improvements demonstrate usefulness but do not establish that the cause is learning diverse invariant features. Selected Grad-CAM images are not quantitative evidence of feature reliance, and unnormalized top Hessian eigenvalues without uncertainty neither establish a common flat minimum nor connect flatness to feature diversity.

Algorithmically, ASGDRO is a fairly direct combination of adaptive sharpness-aware optimization and GDRO. The paper lacks decisive ablations separating adaptive scaling, sharpness regularization, and group reweighting, and H-CMNIST compares against only ERM, ASAM, and GDRO rather than other feature-diversification, masking, or augmentation approaches. Together with the invalid core theorem, this makes the originality and mechanistic support insufficient for acceptance despite promising results.

Reproducibility details are uneven: WILDS training and model-selection protocols are largely unspecified, most subpopulation baselines are imported despite substantial tuning of ASGDRO, and the CMNIST appendix says the test correlation is flipped but then describes the same class-color direction as training. The manuscript also promises sensitivity and efficiency analyses that are not present; these are secondary presentation/reporting issues rather than the main reason for rejection.

Because the convex weights sum to one, every θ_lambda predicts the same value; consequently, its MSE, gradient norm, and exact worst-case loss under an L2 parameter ball are independent of lambda. The proof introduces lambda elementwise-multiplied by the gradient without justification and then uses a norm factorization that is not generally valid, so the claimed unique uniform solution does not follow.

The central bridge from SIL to flatness is unsupported. Even if every invariant mechanism lies within distance rho, the maximum risk over those finitely many mechanisms is only bounded by—not equal to—the maximum over the entire parameter ball. Arbitrary parameter perturbations need not correspond to changing invariant features, so parameter-space flatness does not establish feature diversity. Proposition 1 also equates small first-order gradient norm with flatness even though both sharp and flat stationary minima have zero gradient.

The SIL definitions require assumptions not supplied by Definition 1. Invariance conditioned on the complete feature set does not imply invariance or predictive sufficiency for every subset or singleton. The maximum over all subsets is ambiguous about the empty set, the operation h(Z_hat) under missing inputs is undefined, and Appendix A.2's singleton reduction assumes rather than proves that adding features cannot hurt.

The implementation analyzed experimentally differs materially from the proposed objective: except in the toy example, it replaces the environment-specific adversarial perturbations with one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. No result shows that this approximation retains common per-environment flatness or the asserted SIL property.

Only synthetic H-CMNIST directly tests loss of an invariant cue, and it contains just two designed cues; ASGDRO's shape-only result also has substantial three-seed variability. Standard spurious-correlation and domain-shift benchmarks do not test missing invariant features. Grad-CAM is qualitative and cannot establish causal reliance on multiple cues, while lower Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate the optimized flatness property rather than its claimed connection to SIL.

Important controls are absent: there is no comparison of the theoretical environment-specific perturbation against the practical common perturbation, no quantitative measure of learned feature diversity, and no sensitivity or efficiency study despite the main text saying these are in the appendix. Several gains are small relative to reported variation, and no significance testing is given.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are uneven. Many baseline numbers are imported from other papers, WILDS and original-ASGDRO DomainBed training details are incomplete, and original DomainBed results lack error bars. ASGDRO also requires roughly two forward/backward passes, but its actual time and memory costs are not reported. These issues are secondary to the invalid core theory, which makes the current balance favor rejection despite worthwhile empirical evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and intuitive failure mode: invariant predictors may still be brittle when they rely on only one of several valid cues and that cue becomes unavailable. The SIL framing usefully emphasizes redundancy among invariant features.

ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically relevant. It combines group-robust weighting with adaptive sharpness-aware optimization, while the shared-perturbation implementation limits the sharpness step to two passes per iteration rather than one per environment.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. It covers a purpose-built H-CMNIST test, four subpopulation-shift datasets, multiple WILDS datasets, and five DomainBed datasets. Results are consistently competitive; for example, ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44±1.03 to 69.17±6.19 and improves DPLCLIP's training-domain-selected DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0.

The H-CMNIST intervention directly removes the easy color cue and therefore tests the intended behavior more directly than ordinary aggregate OOD accuracy. Component baselines—ERM, ASAM, and GDRO—help isolate the value of combining sharpness awareness with group robustness.

The motivation and figures are generally clear, and the appendix reports architectures, optimizers, hyperparameter ranges, seeds, hardware, and a code URL, supporting reproducibility. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1_sk4vus/call-69b9acb590654dd995f49ddafea04226/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Theorem 1, which is central to the claimed SIL mechanism, is incorrect as stated. Under its assumptions, Z=(1,…,1), θλ=λ, and ∑iλi=1. An additive perturbation produces prediction 1+1ᵀε, so the exact worst-case MSE over ||ε||≤ρ is independent of λ and cannot prefer uniform weights. The proof inserts λ⊙∇R without deriving it from the stated Euclidean perturbation objective; moreover, when Y=1, the first-order gradient is zero for every λ. Thus the theorem does not establish that ASGDRO balances invariant features.

Proposition 1 is only the standard first-order SAM approximation. A small gradient denotes stationarity, not flatness, and the proposition proves neither convergence to a common flat minimum nor acquisition of diverse invariant mechanisms. The appendix's spurious-feature argument additionally assumes without justification that high-loss, highly activated neurons encode spurious rather than invariant information.

The evaluated algorithm differs materially from the analyzed objective. Equation (3) and the theory use a separately maximized perturbation for every environment, whereas all non-toy experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel in this shared perturbation, so it need not maximize or control each group loss. No comparison between the analyzed and implemented variants is provided.

The SIL formalization has unresolved issues: its maximum over all subsets includes the empty subset, its classifier input under different feature subsets is not formally defined, and it optimizes over all environments E even though unseen environments are unavailable. Appendix A.2 silently excludes the empty subset and reduces the objective to singleton subsets using the unproven assumption that adding features cannot hurt a fixed classifier. The claimed “without loss of generality” representation of multi-feature mechanisms as convex interpolations of singleton mechanisms is also unjustified for nonlinear networks.

Only H-CMNIST directly measures performance after removing an invariant cue. The standard benchmarks establish useful OOD accuracy but do not identify multiple invariant cues or show that ASGDRO uses them. Selected Grad-CAM images are not causal evidence of feature reliance, while the Hessian study reports only two eigenvalues without seed uncertainty or scale-normalized analysis and does not connect flatness quantitatively to cue diversity.

Important evaluation controls are missing: environment-specific versus shared perturbations, adaptive versus ordinary sharpness, sensitivity to ρ, matched tuning budgets, and runtime/memory measurements. Several comparisons reuse numbers from other papers while ASGDRO receives substantial tuning. H-CMNIST dataset sizes and model-selection protocol are not reported, results use only three seeds, and the promised sensitivity/efficiency analysis is absent from the appendix.

The SIL perspective is potentially original, but ASGDRO itself is largely a direct composition of ASAM-style perturbations and GDRO weighting. With the central theoretical link unsupported and the mechanistic evidence limited, the remaining contribution is a promising but incremental optimizer with strong empirical results; this balance favors weak rejection rather than acceptance. Minor notation and prose issues are secondary to these scientific concerns.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful robustness failure mode: a model may learn one invariant cue yet fail when that cue is absent. H-CMNIST operationalizes this distinction between suppressing a spurious feature and learning multiple predictive cues. The manuscript is generally clear and well illustrated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1bepfb6t/call-6fcca17ed97242f9996124f234791579/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

ASGDRO is a simple, model-agnostic synthesis of adaptive sharpness-aware training and GroupDRO. Its practical shared-perturbation variant limits the sharpness step to one computation irrespective of the number of groups.

The empirical study is broad, covering H-CMNIST, four subpopulation-shift datasets, WILDS, and five DomainBed datasets. Improvements over GDRO include 69.17 versus 61.44 shape-only accuracy on H-CMNIST, 91.0 versus 87.2 worst-group accuracy on CelebA, and 74.0 versus 72.9 average DomainBed accuracy when integrated with DPLCLIP.

Comparisons among ERM, ASAM, GDRO, and ASGDRO provide a useful partial factorial analysis: sharpness awareness alone does not address spurious correlations, while adding it to group robustness often improves results. Hyperparameter grids, seed counts, hardware, and a code link are also provided.
weaknesses: The SIL formulation is not technically sound under the stated assumptions. Invariance of the joint set, E[Y|Z^I] being stable, does not imply invariance or predictive sufficiency of every subset or singleton. Definition 3 even maximizes over all subsets, nominally including the empty set. It therefore demands that every individual feature predict the target, excluding complementary or interaction-based features such as XOR. The assertion that arbitrary subset mechanisms can, without loss of generality, be represented by interpolating singleton mechanisms is false for general nonlinear predictors.

Theorem 1 is false as written. In its own setting, let Z=(1,...,1), sum_i lambda_i=1, and use squared loss. For any Euclidean perturbation ball, max_{||epsilon||<=rho} (Y-sum_i(lambda_i+epsilon_i))^2/2 is independent of lambda; when Y=1 it equals rho^2 p/2. Thus the objective cannot uniquely prefer lambda=(1/p,...,1/p). The proof introduces lambda elementwise-multiplied with the gradient without justification and then uses a norm factorization that does not generally hold. This invalidates the main claimed theoretical mechanism for balancing invariant features.

The bridge from invariant mechanisms to parameter-space flatness is unsubstantiated. If a ball contains the hypothetical singleton mechanisms, its maximum risk is only bounded below by their maximum; it is not equal because the ball contains many unrelated directions. Mode connectivity between some fine-tuned models does not establish that missing-feature mechanisms lie in such a ball or that all intervening parameters have low loss.

There is a consequential mismatch between theory and experiments. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separately optimized perturbation for each environment, whereas almost all experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. A shared direction can miss the sharp direction of an individual environment, so the experiments do not optimize the analyzed common-flatness objective. The theorem also analyzes an ordinary Euclidean ball while the method uses parameter-dependent adaptive normalization.

Proposition 1 is only a first-order SAM approximation and does not establish flatness: gradients vanish at both sharp and flat differentiable minima, where second-order terms dominate. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes without support that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious features; neither suppressing such neurons nor reducing curvature proves removal of spurious information or generalization when invariant cues disappear.

The evidence supports ASGDRO as a potentially useful optimizer but not its proposed SIL explanation. Only synthetic H-CMNIST directly removes an invariant cue, and it uses just four baselines with three seeds and relatively large ASGDRO variance. Standard shift benchmarks do not test missing invariant features. Curated Grad-CAM maps are neither quantitative nor causal evidence of feature diversity, while smaller Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate local curvature—not use of multiple invariant mechanisms.

Several attribution and reproducibility gaps remain: there is no ablation of ordinary SAM+GDRO versus adaptive normalization, shared versus per-environment perturbations, or the individual design choices; many baselines are imported rather than rerun; exact selected hyperparameters and H-CMNIST sample sizes/model-selection protocol are omitted; and the promised sensitivity and efficiency analyses do not appear in the appendix. The two-pass training overhead is acknowledged but not measured.

The empirical gains and useful problem framing constitute worthwhile merit, but the false central theorem, ill-posed definition, theory–implementation mismatch, and lack of direct real-data evidence for SIL are material scientific weaknesses rather than presentation refinements. The balance therefore favors weak rejection.

strengths: The missing-invariant-cue problem is important and intuitively motivated: models should exploit redundant predictive cues so that occlusion, cropping, or other shifts do not eliminate their sole decision mechanism.
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically relevant, combining group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware training.

The evaluation is broad, spanning H-CMNIST, four subpopulation benchmarks, WILDS, and DomainBed. Reported results include meaningful gains, such as 69.17% versus GDRO's 61.44% on the H-CMNIST shape-only test and 74.0 versus 72.9 average accuracy for DPLCLIP+ASGDRO versus DPLCLIP+GDRO.
The paper includes useful component baselines, several three-seed error bars, hyperparameter ranges for major experiments, qualitative attention visualizations, Hessian diagnostics, and a code URL.
weaknesses: Material: the SIL formalization rests on a false premise. Joint invariance of E[Y|Z^I] does not imply invariance or predictiveness for every subset of Z^I; changing the distribution of omitted features can change E[Y|Z_i^I]. Feature interactions can also make no singleton predictive. Appendix A.2 merely assumes that additional features never hurt and does not establish the claimed reduction to singleton subsets.

Material: the bridge from semantic feature diversity to weight-space flatness is unjustified. The asserted equality max_i R^e(theta_i^I)=max_{||epsilon||<=rho} R^e(theta^SI+epsilon) is generally false because the ball contains arbitrary parameter directions, not just invariant mechanisms. Likewise, nonlinear mechanisms for feature subsets cannot, without loss of generality, be represented by convex interpolation of singleton mechanisms.

Material: Theorem 1 is incorrect under its own assumptions. With Z=(1,...,1) and simplex weights lambda, every theta_lambda predicts sum_i lambda_i=1. The exact worst-case MSE after an L2-bounded perturbation therefore depends on Y, p, and rho but not on lambda, so it cannot uniquely select uniform weights. The proof introduces a lambda-weighted gradient term that does not follow from the stated MSE gradient. This invalidates the principal theoretical claim that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms.

Material: Proposition 1 is only a first-order SAM approximation and cannot prove convergence to flat minima; the gradient is zero at both sharp and flat stationary minima. Appendix A.5 is also heuristic rather than a proof of spurious-feature removal: high environment loss does not imply that active neurons encode spurious information, nor is the proposed suppression selective for spurious rather than invariant features.

Material: the algorithm analyzed is not the one used in nearly all experiments. Equation (3) uses a separate worst-case perturbation for each environment, whereas the implementation uses one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Group-specific sharp directions can cancel in that average, so the common-flatness theory does not apply to the reported implementation. Adaptive parameter scaling is another difference not covered by the theorem.

Material: only synthetic H-CMNIST directly tests removal of an invariant cue, and it compares just four methods over three seeds; its central shape-only result also has a large standard deviation. Standard subpopulation and domain benchmarks demonstrate ordinary robustness but do not establish that multiple invariant mechanisms were learned. Selected Grad-CAM examples are not causal measurements of cue usage, while lower Hessian eigenvalues establish neither feature diversity nor SIL.

Material: the empirical attribution is incomplete. ASGDRO is effectively an ASAM-style perturbation combined with GDRO, yet there is no ablation of adaptive versus ordinary perturbations, per-environment versus common perturbations, or the individual objective choices. Several improvements are within reported variability, and ASGDRO is not strongest on CivilComments. Thus the broad results support a potentially useful training heuristic but not the stronger mechanism and generality claims.

Presentation/reproducibility: important H-CMNIST split and generation details, WILDS settings, Hessian protocol, and some auxiliary-dataset settings are absent. The manuscript promises efficiency and sensitivity analyses that do not appear in the appendix. Notational inconsistencies and grammatical issues are secondary; the rejection recommendation is driven by the central theoretical errors and theory-experiment mismatch.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and intuitive failure mode: a model can learn an invariant cue yet fail when that particular cue is absent. Framing robustness around redundant invariant evidence is potentially useful.

H-CMNIST provides a controlled evaluation that separately removes the easy color cue and reverses the box-position shortcut. ASGDRO improves TestBed-2 shape-only accuracy from 61.44% for GDRO to 69.17%, offering direct, albeit synthetic, evidence for the proposed motivation.

ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and empirically promising. It improves worst-group accuracy over GDRO on CMNIST, Waterbirds, and CelebA, and improves DPLCLIP's five-dataset DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0 under training-domain model selection.

The evaluation spans subpopulation and domain shifts, multiple vision datasets, and several diagnostic views. Comparisons among ERM, ASAM, GDRO, and ASGDRO help show that neither sharpness awareness nor group robustness alone explains all reported gains.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, includes pseudocode and extensive hyperparameter information, reports uncertainty for most new results, and provides a code link.
weaknesses: The central Theorem 1 is not technically valid as proved. Proposition 1 yields a term proportional to ||∇R(θλ)||, but Appendix A.4 replaces this without justification by ||-λ⊙∇R(θλ)||. Under the theorem's own setting, θλ=λ, Z=(1,...,1), and Σi λi=1, so the MSE prediction and its parameter gradient are identical for every feasible λ; the objective therefore cannot select the uniform vector (1/p,...,1/p). Consequently, the claimed theoretical guarantee that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms does not follow.

The common-flat-minimum argument is also insufficient. A first-order approximation gives R+ρ||∇R||, but a small gradient does not establish flatness because both sharp and flat differentiable minima have zero gradient. Moreover, minimizing a maximum of risk-plus-gradient terms does not show that each environment attains a shared flat minimum. These are material theoretical gaps rather than presentation issues.

The SIL definition requires robustness to every subset of invariant features, although invariance does not imply that each feature is individually predictive or sufficient. The written subset maximum also includes the empty set, which Appendix A.2 silently omits, and the reduction to singleton subsets assumes rather than derives monotonic performance when features are added. Thus SIL can be infeasible under Definition 1 and is not well formalized for a classifier receiving different feature subsets.

There is a material mismatch between the analyzed method and the implemented one. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separate adversarial perturbation for each environment, whereas Section 3.5 states that nearly all experiments use one perturbation computed from aggregate empirical risk. The theory therefore does not cover the algorithm producing the reported results.

Only H-CMNIST directly evaluates robustness after removing an invariant cue, and its ASGDRO result has substantial three-seed variability (69.17±6.19). The real-data benchmarks primarily evaluate shortcut removal or ordinary domain generalization; improved worst-group accuracy, selected Grad-CAM examples, and lower Hessian eigenvalues do not demonstrate that multiple distinct invariant cues were learned or caused the gains.

The algorithmic novelty is limited because ASGDRO is largely a combination of adaptive sharpness-aware optimization and GroupDRO. The paper lacks decisive comparisons or ablations against natural alternatives such as applying SAM/ASAM directly to the GroupDRO objective, per-environment versus shared perturbations, and closely related sharpness-aware domain-generalization methods cited in the manuscript, including SAGM and flatness-aware minimization.

Secondary reproducibility and presentation issues include sparse WILDS training details and an internal RxRx1 discrepancy: Table 3 reports 32.2±0.2 for ASGDRO, while Figure 7 reports 30.5±0.1. These are correctable, but the invalid central theorem and weak empirical validation of the claimed SIL mechanism make the current balance favor rejection despite the promising benchmark results.

strengths: The SIL framing highlights an important failure mode: a model may suppress spurious correlations yet remain brittle when its preferred invariant cue is missing or occluded. This is relevant to robust visual recognition and clearly motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-zo3girqw/call-3f47fe1ef61940569be7fa28fdbfce5c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically useful: it combines adaptive sharpness-aware optimization with group-robust reweighting and can be integrated with methods such as DPLCLIP.

The controlled H-CMNIST experiment directly probes retention of a harder invariant feature. On the shape-only test, ASGDRO reaches 69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03 for GDRO and 57.41±2.58 for ERM, while preserving near-perfect TestBed-1 performance.

The empirical coverage is broad. ASGDRO obtains the best or tied-best worst-group accuracy on CMNIST, Waterbirds, and CelebA, remains competitive on CivilComments, improves all five reported WILDS metrics, and raises DPLCLIP's DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0 under training-domain model selection.

The manuscript is readable and provides useful diagnostics through Grad-CAM and Hessian analyses. It also reports three-seed deviations, hyperparameter ranges for several experiments, hardware, pseudocode, and a public code link.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 appears incorrect under its stated assumptions. With Z=(1,…,1), θλ a convex combination satisfying Σλi=1, and singleton mechanisms optimal for the MSE target 1, every θλ has zero gradient and the exact isotropic-neighborhood maximum is ρ²p/2, independent of λ; it therefore cannot select λi=1/p. The proof also introduces λ⊙∇R without deriving it from Proposition 1 and factorizes its norm unjustifiably. Likewise, a small gradient norm alone does not imply flatness at a stationary point. This materially weakens the claimed theoretical explanation.

The SIL formalization relies on unsupported assumptions. Conditional invariance given the full feature set is not generally inherited by every subset, and an arbitrary subset need not support an optimal classifier. The main definition also includes the empty subset, while the appendix silently excludes it and reduces all subsets to singletons by assuming that additional features never hurt. Parameter interpolation between singleton mechanisms is not equivalent to feature-subset interpolation for nonlinear networks.

The analyzed and implemented objectives differ substantially. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separately optimized perturbation for every environment, whereas almost all experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. That shared direction need not expose each group's sharp directions, and no result establishes that the theory applies to this computational shortcut.

Only H-CMNIST directly evaluates missing invariant cues, and it is a single synthetic construction with three seeds and relatively high ASGDRO variance. Standard subpopulation and domain-shift benchmarks demonstrate utility but do not identify diverse invariant mechanisms. Grad-CAM coverage is qualitative rather than causal, while lower Hessian eigenvalues establish neither feature diversity nor SIL.

The algorithmic novelty is modest because the practical method is largely an ASAM–GDRO composition. Ablations comparing adaptive versus ordinary SAM, environment-specific versus shared perturbations, and the full method against a simpler SAM+GDRO composition are needed to substantiate which design choices cause the gains.

Reproducibility is uneven despite the code release: WILDS training and model-selection details are sparse, several comparisons use numbers imported from other papers rather than controlled reruns, Hessian/Grad-CAM sampling protocols are unspecified, and the claimed appendix efficiency and sensitivity studies are absent. The doubled forward/backward cost is acknowledged but not measured.

The manuscript reports multiple seeds, error bars, architectures, substantial hyperparameter ranges, computational limitations, and a code link. Its organization and visual presentation are generally clear.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect under its own assumptions. With Z=(1,…,1), θλ=λ, Σiλi=1, and squared loss, R(θλ)=0.5(Y−1)^2 and the exact perturbed risk max_{||ε||≤ρ}R(θλ+ε) are independent of how mass is distributed among the λi. Thus all λ on the simplex tie; ASGDRO does not uniquely select λ=(1/p,…,1/p). The proof introduces λ⊙∇R without justification and uses a generally false factorization of its norm. This invalidates the main claimed guarantee that flatness balances invariant mechanisms.

The foundations of SIL are not established. Invariance of the joint feature set ZI does not imply invariance—or label sufficiency—of every subset, contrary to Section 3.2. Definition 3 also maximizes over all subsets, apparently including the empty set, whereas Appendix A.2 silently excludes it and relies on an unverified assumption that adding features cannot hurt.

The central bridge from SIL to sharpness is unjustified. Even if hypothetical singleton-mechanism parameters lie inside a radius-ρ ball, their maximum risk is only bounded by the maximum over that ball, not equal to it. Arbitrary parameter perturbations do not correspond to removing invariant features, and representing multi-feature mechanisms as weight-space interpolations of singleton mechanisms is not without loss of generality for deep networks.

Proposition 1 is merely a first-order SAM approximation; a small gradient at a stationary point does not establish low curvature or flatness. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes without proof that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious features and does not show that its update necessarily suppresses them.

The analyzed objective uses a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, but all substantive experiments use one perturbation computed from aggregate empirical risk. Group gradients can cancel in this implementation, so the theory does not establish that the evaluated algorithm finds a common flat minimum.

Only H-CMNIST directly tests survival after removing an invariant cue, and it is synthetic with three seeds and substantial ASGDRO variance (e.g., 69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03). The constructed toy landscape is illustrative rather than evidence about learned features. Ordinary benchmark accuracy, selected Grad-CAM examples, and raw Hessian eigenvalues do not demonstrate that multiple distinct invariant mechanisms were learned.

The experiments lack decisive attribution controls: group DRO combined with ordinary SAM, adaptive versus non-adaptive perturbations, per-environment versus shared perturbations, equal-compute controls, and feature-masking or diversity-promoting baselines. Comparisons to the closest cited sharpness-aware domain-generalization methods are also incomplete, leaving unclear whether the gains reflect SIL rather than generic SAM regularization and extra computation.

Several results are modest or mixed—CelebA worst-group accuracy ties PDE, CivilComments is below LISA, and many baselines are copied from other sources. WILDS training/model-selection details and exact H-CMNIST sizes and generation procedure are insufficiently specified in the manuscript. Overall, the empirical promise is worthwhile, but the incorrect theorem and unsupported mechanism claim make the current balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant failure mode: a model may learn one invariant cue that is unavailable at test time. The SIL framing and H-CMNIST benchmark communicate this motivation clearly.
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and compatible with existing methods such as DPLCLIP.

The evaluation is broad. ASGDRO improves GDRO on H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy (69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03), Waterbirds worst-group accuracy (91.4 versus 90.6), and the five-dataset DPLCLIP average (74.0 versus 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO).
The manuscript provides architectures, hyperparameter ranges, seed counts, a code URL, qualitative visualizations, and Hessian diagnostics.
weaknesses: Material technical flaw: Theorem 1 is false under its stated perturbation. For Z=(1,...,1), θλ=(λ1,...,λp), and Σiλi=1, the stated MSE after perturbation is 1/2(Y−1−Σiεi)^2. Its maximum over ||ε||≤ρ is independent of λ, so every convex combination is optimal—not uniquely the uniform one. The proof introduces −λ⊙∇R without justification. This invalidates the main claimed guarantee that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms.

The reduction motivating ASGDRO is unsupported. A ball containing the singleton mechanisms only gives max_ball R≥max_i R(θ_i), not the equality asserted in Section 3.3. Likewise, representing arbitrary feature-subset mechanisms as parameter interpolations is not “without loss of generality,” especially for nonlinear networks; Appendix A.2 does not prove this claim.

Proposition 1 does not establish convergence to flat minima or diverse features. The gradient vanishes at both sharp and flat differentiable minima, while curvature is a second-order property. More fundamentally, parameter-space flatness does not imply that a predictor uses multiple semantic cues. The reported Hessian eigenvalues and selected Grad-CAM examples cannot establish that causal link.

There is a consequential theory–implementation mismatch: the objective and Algorithm 1 use a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, whereas all substantive experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. No bound or ablation shows that this practical update finds the claimed common flat minimum. Algorithmically, it is largely an ASAM-style perturbation combined with GDRO weighting, without comparisons to SAM+GDRO, per-environment perturbations, or other feature-diversification methods.

Direct evidence for SIL is narrow. Only synthetic H-CMNIST explicitly removes an invariant feature, it includes four baselines and three seeds, and ASGDRO's key shape-only result has substantial variability. The standard distribution-shift benchmarks do not test invariant-feature disappearance, while the real-image evidence is qualitative rather than a systematic occlusion or intervention evaluation.

Several reporting issues impede reproducibility: Table 3 reports ASGDRO RxRx1 accuracy as 32.2±0.2, whereas Figure 7 reports 30.5±0.1; the appendix describes the CMNIST test color proportions as preserving rather than flipping the training correlation; and H-CMNIST split sizes, validation/model-selection protocol, and Hessian-estimation details are omitted. These are secondary to the theoretical problems but still require correction.

The evaluation is broad and contains encouraging results. Examples include 69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03 for GDRO on H-CMNIST's shape-only test, 91.4±0.1 versus 90.6±1.1 worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds, and a 74.0 versus 72.9 average when replacing GDRO with ASGDRO in DPLCLIP on DomainBed.
The paper provides a code link, many architectural and hyperparameter details, multi-seed results, and complementary Grad-CAM and Hessian analyses.
weaknesses: Theorem 1, which is central to the claimed connection between flatness and diverse invariant mechanisms, is false under its stated model. With θλ=λ, ∑iλi=1, Z=(1,…,1), and squared loss, both the prediction and residual are independent of λ. If Y=1, the exact sharpness objective is max‖ε‖≤ρ 1/2(∑iεi)²=ρ²p/2 for every λ, so it cannot uniquely prefer λ=(1/p,…,1/p). The proof introduces the factor −λ⊙∇R without justification, contradicting its preceding expression for ∇R.

The SIL formalization assumes properties that do not follow from Definition 1. Invariance of E[Y|ZI] for the joint feature set does not imply invariance—or optimal prediction—for every subset or singleton. Appendix A.2 effectively adds the strong assumptions that every singleton is sufficient and that additional features cannot hurt; the maximum over all subsets is also ambiguous about the empty subset and lacks a defined missing-feature intervention. This undermines the claimed generality of SIL.

The analyzed objective and implemented method differ materially. Equation 3, Algorithm 1, and the theoretical discussion use an independently maximized perturbation εe for every environment, whereas Section 3.5 states that all non-toy experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Consequently, the theory does not establish the properties of the algorithm producing the reported results.

Proposition 1 is only a first-order Taylor approximation, and a small gradient at a solution does not establish flatness: both sharp and flat differentiable minima have zero gradient. Reporting two raw Hessian eigenvalues per group shows reduced local curvature but neither a common loss basin nor use of diverse features, and raw parameter-space curvature is sensitive to reparameterization.

Evidence for SIL specifically is limited. Only the synthetic H-CMNIST experiment directly removes an invariant cue; its shape-only result has high variability over three seeds and remains only 69.17%. The standard subpopulation and domain benchmarks measure shortcut or domain robustness rather than resilience to missing invariant features. Selected Grad-CAM maps are qualitative and cannot establish causal reliance on multiple cues.

ASGDRO is close to a direct composition of adaptive SAM and GroupDRO, but there is no controlled ablation of standard versus adaptive perturbations, per-environment versus shared perturbations, or equal-compute GroupDRO-plus-SAM variants. Closely related cited sharpness-aware domain-generalization methods are not consistently included, limiting both originality assessment and attribution of the gains to the proposed mechanism.

Several reporting issues weaken reproducibility: Figure 7 gives 30.5±0.1 for ASGDRO on RxRx1 while Table 3 gives 32.2±0.2; WILDS training and model-selection details are sparse; many baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun uniformly; and the promised efficiency and sensitivity analyses are absent from the appendix. These are secondary to the theoretical problems, but reinforce a weak-reject assessment.

strengths: The paper identifies an intuitive and practically relevant failure mode: a model may learn an invariant feature that is unavailable at test time. Framing robustness as learning redundant/diverse predictive cues is potentially useful for computer vision.

ASGDRO is simple and model-agnostic, combining group robustness with sharpness-aware optimization. It consistently improves over GDRO in the reported direct comparisons: worst-group accuracy rises from 68.6 to 74.2 on CMNIST, 90.6 to 91.4 on Waterbirds, 87.2 to 91.0 on CelebA, and 70.0 to 71.8 on CivilComments.

H-CMNIST directly probes performance after removing the easy color cue. ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy from 61.44±1.03 for GDRO to 69.17±6.19, providing some evidence that the method encourages use of the harder feature.

The evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic data, subpopulation shifts, WILDS, and DomainBed. Applying ASGDRO to DPLCLIP improves the training-domain-selection average from 72.6 to 74.0, suggesting practical compatibility with a strong pretrained method.

The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies pseudocode, many hyperparameter ranges, hardware information, error bars for several experiments, qualitative visualizations, and a public code link.
weaknesses: Theorem 1, which is central to the claimed connection between ASGDRO and balanced invariant-feature use, appears mathematically incorrect. Under its own setup, Z=(1,...,1), θλ=(λ1,...,λp), and Σiλi=1 imply that the prediction, risk, and gradient ∇R(θλ)=-(Y-1)1 are all independent of λ. The exact sharpness objective is consequently also independent of λ. The proof introduces λ⊙∇R without justification and therefore cannot conclude that λ=(1/p,...,1/p) is uniquely preferred.

The SIL formalization relies on unsupported assumptions. Conditional invariance given the full feature set does not imply invariance for every subset; for example, marginalizing one variable in a stable two-feature mechanism can produce environment-dependent P(Y|Z1). Nor must every singleton invariant feature predict the label. Thus the singleton mechanisms used throughout may not exist. Appendix A.2 assumes monotonic benefit from additional observed features but does not establish these claims or the asserted equivalence between feature subsets and parameter interpolations.

The bridge from parameter-space flatness to diverse feature use is not demonstrated. The equality between the maximum risk over finitely many invariant mechanisms and the maximum over an entire parameter ball is unjustified; at most one obtains an inequality if all mechanisms lie in that ball. Moreover, a small first-order gradient is not evidence of flatness at a stationary point, since both sharp and flat minima have zero gradient. The argument in Appendix A.5 that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious features is likewise asserted rather than proved.

The analyzed objective does not match the implemented method. The theory uses per-environment Euclidean adversarial perturbations, Algorithm 1 introduces adaptive parameter scaling, and the practical implementation instead computes one shared perturbation from average empirical risk. Gradient cancellation can make this shared perturbation very different from the per-environment worst-case perturbations needed by the analysis.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed ingredient. ASGDRO is largely a combination of ASAM and GDRO, yet there is no GDRO+SAM, GDRO+ASAM, per-environment-versus-shared-perturbation, or compute-matched ablation. Comparing only ASAM and GDRO separately cannot show whether adaptivity, group-specific sharpness, or a generic two-pass regularizer causes the gains.

Evidence for the headline mechanism outside H-CMNIST is weak. Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and unquantified, while lower Hessian eigenvalues establish neither semantic feature diversity nor robustness to missing features. The real-data experiments measure ordinary OOD accuracy without controlled removal of distinct invariant attributes. H-CMNIST uses only three seeds and has substantial variance in its decisive results.

Reproducibility and reporting remain incomplete: WILDS training and model-selection details are underspecified, statistical significance is not analyzed, and the text promises efficiency and sensitivity experiments that do not appear in the appendix. The acknowledged two-forward/two-backward-pass cost is also not quantified. These issues are secondary to the invalid central theory but further weaken the empirical attribution.

Overall, the consistent benchmark gains are worthwhile, but the paper presents them as validation of SIL through common flat minima without establishing that causal or theoretical link. Because the principal theorem and several foundational assumptions fail, the evidence currently supports a potentially useful empirical optimizer more than the claimed scientific contribution.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-clw4eosn/call-b028b80f27a742e78af73f1f982b97a3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} identifies an important failure mode: a predictor may discard spurious correlations yet remain brittle because it relies on only one of several invariant cues. The SIL framing and H-CMNIST construction make this issue intuitive and relevant to visual recognition under occlusion or missing attributes.

ASGDRO is model-agnostic and straightforward to implement, combining group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware perturbations. Its integration with DPLCLIP usefully demonstrates compatibility with another domain-generalization method.

The evaluation is broad: H-CMNIST, four subpopulation-shift datasets, five WILDS datasets, and five DomainBed datasets. Results are often competitive—for example, ASGDRO obtains 69.17±6.19 versus GDRO's 61.44±1.03 on H-CMNIST TestBed 2, and DPLCLIP+ASGDRO improves the training-domain-validation DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0.

The appendix supplies dataset protocols, search spaces, architectures, hardware, three-seed error bars, qualitative Grad-CAM results, Hessian measurements, and a code link. This is appreciably more reproducibility information than appears in the main text.
weaknesses: Material technical flaw: Theorem 1 is not valid as stated. With the specified linear MSE model, every convex combination θλ has the same coordinate sum, so both its prediction and its worst-case loss under the stated Euclidean perturbation are independent of λ. The proof nevertheless introduces an unexplained λ⊙∇R term and concludes that minimizing the objective selects uniform λ. Consequently, the claimed guarantee that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms does not follow.

Material conceptual gap: SIL optimizes over all environments—including unseen ones—and every subset of invariant features, although invariance is defined only over training environments. The reduction from arbitrary subsets to singletons relies on an assumed monotonicity of loss when features are added, ignores the empty subset, and does not establish that weight-space interpolation of deep networks corresponds to combining feature mechanisms. Thus the formalism does not bridge training-time flatness to robustness under missing invariant cues.

Material objective–implementation mismatch: Eq. (3) and the theory use a separately maximized perturbation εe for each environment, whereas all substantive experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. These are not equivalent; opposing group gradients can cancel in the shared perturbation even when individual group losses are sharp. The common-flatness argument therefore does not directly apply to the evaluated algorithm.

The principal SIL claim has limited direct evidence. Only synthetic H-CMNIST explicitly removes an invariant cue, uses just three seeds, and has high variance for ASGDRO. Standard subpopulation, WILDS, and DomainBed accuracy does not show that multiple invariant cues were learned. Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and not a reliable measure of feature use, while two Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate neither cue diversity nor robustness to cue removal.

The method is largely the natural composition of adaptive SAM and GDRO, while prior work already connects SAM with balanced feature learning and flatness with domain generalization. There is no ablation against non-adaptive SAM+GDRO, per-environment versus shared perturbations, or other controls that isolate which component causes the reported gains. Hence the originality case depends heavily on the unsupported SIL interpretation.

Several comparisons mix newly tuned ASGDRO runs with numbers imported from prior work, despite ASGDRO receiving searches over ρ, group-update rate, adjusted-group coefficient, learning rate, regularization, and sometimes batch size. Statistical testing is absent, selected hyperparameters and H-CMNIST model-selection criteria are not reported, and some gains are small relative to variability. These are secondary and potentially correctable issues, but the invalid central theorem and missing evidence connecting ASGDRO to SIL currently make the balance favor rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies an important failure mode—models may depend on only one of several invariant cues—and motivates it clearly. H-CMNIST is a useful controlled attempt to measure robustness when an easier invariant cue is removed. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ti9dn7ny/call-cc7a7b45a72940cb872e510a39d963d0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically relevant: it combines group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware updates and can be integrated into methods such as DPLCLIP.

The empirical coverage is broad. On H-CMNIST, ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy from 61.44±1.03 for GDRO to 69.17±6.19; it also obtains strong worst-group results on CMNIST, Waterbirds, and CelebA. With training-domain model selection, DPLCLIP+ASGDRO averages 74.0 on DomainBed versus 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO and 72.6 for DPLCLIP.

The comparison against both ASAM and GDRO provides some evidence that sharpness control and group robustness are complementary. Grad-CAM and Hessian measurements are also directionally consistent with the proposed interpretation.
The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear, provides code, reports three-seed uncertainty for many experiments, and documents several hyperparameter grids and hardware settings.
weaknesses: Material—the SIL definition is not technically well-founded. It optimizes over all environments E although only E_tr is available; it does not define how one classifier consumes arbitrary feature subsets; and invariance of E[Y|Z^I] does not imply invariance or predictive sufficiency of every subset. Requiring good prediction from every singleton additionally assumes redundant cues, which is substantially stronger than invariance and is not formalized.

Material—Theorem 1 is invalid as written. Under its stated Euclidean perturbation ball, the first-order penalty is ρ||∇R||. For Z=(1,…,1), θ_λ=λ, and Σ_i λ_i=1, both the linear prediction and MSE gradient are independent of λ. The proof introduces −λ⊙∇R without justification, so the conclusion that the uniform λ minimizes the objective does not follow.

Material—the bridge from parameter-space flatness to invariant-feature diversity is largely assumed. The equality between the maximum risk of the finite mechanisms and the maximum over an enclosing parameter ball is generally only an inequality; linear interpolation between mechanisms is not guaranteed; and flat directions can arise from neural-network symmetries without representing alternative invariant cues. Proposition 1 is the standard first-order SAM approximation, while a small gradient at a stationary point does not distinguish sharp from flat minima. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, rather than proves, that high-loss activated neurons encode spurious information.

Material—the method analyzed is not the method used in nearly all experiments. Equation (3) and the theory use separate Euclidean adversarial perturbations for each environment, whereas the implementation uses adaptive normalization and one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel, so this common perturbation need not optimize environment-wise sharpness; consequently, the stated SIL and common-flat-minimum arguments do not apply directly to the evaluated algorithm.

Material—the causal evidence for SIL is limited to one synthetic benchmark, where the key shape-only result has substantial variability across only three seeds. Standard OOD accuracy cannot determine whether gains arise from diverse invariant cues or generic regularization. Grad-CAM is qualitative and non-causal, while unnormalized Hessian eigenvalues are parameterization-dependent and are reported without uncertainty.

Material—the algorithmic novelty is modest because the implemented procedure is essentially an ASAM-style perturbation combined with GDRO weighting. Missing ablations include non-adaptive sharpness-aware GDRO, per-environment versus common perturbations, matched-compute controls, and sensitivity to ρ and γ; despite a statement in the main text, the appendix contains no actual efficiency or sensitivity analysis.

Reporting and reproducibility reservations remain: many comparison numbers are imported from other works, several reported gains are small relative to their deviations, original ASGDRO DomainBed results lack error bars, and WILDS training/model-selection details are incomplete. H-CMNIST sample counts are not specified, and the CMNIST appendix describes its test color correlation as flipped while listing proportions in the same direction as training. These are secondary to the theoretical problems but weaken verification.
