strengths: The manuscript identifies an important and intuitive failure mode: a predictor can be invariant across training environments yet remain brittle when the particular invariant cue it uses becomes unavailable. The bird example communicates this motivation effectively.

ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and potentially useful: it combines group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware training without requiring explicit annotations of individual invariant features.

H-CMNIST provides a controlled test of the central hypothesis. In the shape-only setting, ASGDRO obtains 69.17±6.19 versus 61.44±1.03 for GDRO while retaining approximately 99% performance when the easy color cue is present, offering suggestive evidence that it learns the harder cue.

The empirical study is broad. ASGDRO is competitive on subpopulation-shift datasets and improves DPLCLIP's DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0; the WILDS experiments also report consistent improvements over GDRO.
The paper is generally well organized and includes code, architectures, hyperparameter ranges, three-seed results, group definitions, qualitative visualizations, and an extensive appendix.
weaknesses: Material—Theorem 1 appears mathematically false as stated. With Z=(1,…,1), weights λ summing to one, and squared loss, every λ produces the same prediction. Under the stated Euclidean perturbation, max_{||ε||≤ρ} R(θλ+ε) is independent of λ, so it cannot select λ=(1/p,…,1/p). The proof introduces −λ⊙∇R without justification and then uses a factorization that does not follow from the stated objective. A relative, parameter-scaled perturbation might yield a related result, but that is not the theorem presented.

Material—The reduction from arbitrary invariant-feature subsets to singleton mechanisms is unsupported. Invariance conditional on the full feature set does not imply that every singleton is invariant or individually predictive, and nonlinear feature interactions such as XOR cannot generally be represented by interpolating singleton-model parameters. Appendix A.2's observation-probability argument does not establish the asserted ordering of expected losses.

Material—The claimed implication from flatness to diverse invariant-feature use is not established. The first-order expression R+ρ||∇R|| does not characterize curvature at a stationary point, where both sharp and flat minima have zero gradient. Likewise, generic parameter-space flatness does not ensure that perturbation directions correspond to removing or switching invariant mechanisms.

Material—The experiments do not implement the analyzed objective: except for the toy example, the method uses one perturbation computed from aggregate ERM risk rather than a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment. Group gradients can cancel in this shared perturbation, so the per-environment flatness argument and Algorithm 1 do not directly apply to the reported models.

Material—Only synthetic H-CMNIST directly tests removal of an invariant cue, and even there the conclusion rests on three high-variance runs. Standard subpopulation and domain-shift benchmarks show that the optimizer can improve robustness, but they do not demonstrate that the improvement results from learning multiple invariant mechanisms. The selected Grad-CAM examples and unnormalized Hessian eigenvalues are descriptive, not quantitative evidence of that mechanism.

Material—Algorithmic originality is limited because the practical method is largely a combination of GDRO and ASAM/SAM. The paper lacks component ablations comparing standard versus adaptive sharpness, shared versus per-environment perturbations, and matched sampling/training controls; consequently it does not identify which ingredient causes the gains.

Evaluation/reproducibility—Several comparisons mix newly obtained ASGDRO results with numbers imported from other papers. WILDS training and model-selection details are largely absent, the original DomainBed setup is delegated to another work, and H-CMNIST omits sample counts and a clear model-selection protocol. Several improvements are below one percentage point, yet no significance analysis is provided.

Presentation—Definition 3 optimizes over all environments E, including unavailable test environments, and applies one classifier to unspecified variable feature subsets; the treatment of the empty subset is also unclear. The main text additionally promises efficiency and sensitivity analyses that are not present in the appendix. These issues are repairable, but the incorrect theorem and unsupported central mechanism are decision-driving.

strengths: The manuscript identifies an important failure mode: an invariant predictor may still be brittle when its preferred invariant cue becomes unavailable. The SIL framing and H-CMNIST benchmark provide a useful controlled way to study redundant invariant cues. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vcee51cg/call-94cf813b38194f9fbd809ab01803e9e4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

ASGDRO is a simple, model-agnostic combination of adaptive sharpness-aware optimization and group DRO. Using one common perturbation in practice keeps the extra work independent of the number of environments.

The empirical evaluation is broad. ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44% to 69.17%, Waterbirds worst-group accuracy from 90.6% to 91.4%, and CelebA worst-group accuracy from 87.2% to 91.0%. Adding ASGDRO to DPLCLIP raises the five-dataset DomainBed average from 72.6% to 74.0% under training-domain model selection.
The paper is generally easy to follow and supplies pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, error bars for several experiments, a code link, and complementary Grad-CAM and Hessian diagnostics.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result appears incorrect. Under Theorem 1's stated loss, R(theta)=0.5(Y-sum_i theta_i)^2, the gradient at any convex combination whose coefficients sum to one is independent of how those coefficients are distributed. The proof introduces a lambda-weighted gradient, -lambda elementwise-multiplied by grad R, without justification. Consequently, the sharpness objective in this example does not select the uniform coefficients claimed by the theorem, so the asserted guarantee of balanced invariant mechanisms is unsupported.

Several foundational steps are unjustified. Invariance conditional on the full feature set does not generally imply invariance conditional on every subset. Multi-feature mechanisms also cannot, without loss of generality, be represented by linear interpolation of singleton parameter vectors. Moreover, if the singleton mechanisms lie in a parameter ball, their worst risk is only bounded by the ball's worst risk; it is not equal to it. Appendix A.2 does not establish these claims.

The SIL definition is not operationally precise: it optimizes over all environments, including unseen ones; appears to include the empty feature subset unless implicitly excluded; and applies one classifier to varying feature subsets without defining masking or intervention semantics. Its worst-singleton formulation also requires every invariant feature to be individually predictive, which is stronger than the motivating notion of having a sufficient redundant subset.

Proposition 1 is only a first-order SAM approximation and provides neither approximation conditions nor a bridge from parameter-space flatness to robustness against missing semantic features. Small gradient at one point does not by itself distinguish sharp from flat minima. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, without establishing, that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious information.

The analyzed and evaluated procedures differ materially. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separate adversarial perturbation for every environment, whereas all non-toy experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. The claimed per-environment gradient-norm regularization and common-flatness conclusion therefore do not directly apply to the reported implementation.

Only H-CMNIST directly removes an invariant cue, and its key ASGDRO result uses three seeds with a 6.19-point standard deviation. The standard distribution-shift benchmarks do not test missing invariant features, while the selected Grad-CAM examples and scale-sensitive raw Hessian eigenvalues do not establish semantic feature diversity quantitatively.

Reproducibility and comparison details are incomplete. Many baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun, WILDS training and model-selection settings are not reported, and H-CMNIST sample counts and selection protocol are missing. The promised sensitivity analysis is absent. There is also an unexplained RxRx1 discrepancy: Table 3 reports 32.2±0.2 for ASGDRO, whereas Figure 7 reports 30.5±0.1.

The algorithmic novelty is modest—principally applying adaptive sharpness-aware optimization to group DRO—and it requires two forward/backward passes. Given that the new SIL interpretation is the main conceptual novelty, the invalid central theorem and limited direct evidence currently outweigh the otherwise promising empirical results.

strengths: The paper targets an important failure mode: a model may learn an invariant cue that is absent at test time. The Sufficient Invariant Learning framing is intuitive and relevant to reliable visual recognition.

H-CMNIST provides a controlled test with two invariant cues (color and shape) and one spurious cue (box position). Its shape-only test directly probes the proposed failure mode; ASGDRO obtains 69.17±6.19 versus GDRO's 61.44±1.03.

The evaluation is broad, covering subpopulation shifts, WILDS, and DomainBed. Results are generally favorable: for example, DPLCLIP+ASGDRO averages 74.0 under training-domain model selection, compared with 72.6 for DPLCLIP and 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO.

The groupwise Hessian measurements and Grad-CAM examples are useful supporting diagnostics. The paper also provides an algorithm, hyperparameter ranges, hardware information, three-seed error bars for many experiments, and a code URL.

ASGDRO is model-agnostic and practically simple, combining group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware training; the consistent empirical gains suggest potential usefulness even independently of the SIL interpretation.
weaknesses: Material technical flaw: Theorem 1 is not established and appears false under its own setup. With R(θ)=1/2|Y−Σ_iθ_i|² and θ=λ satisfying Σ_iλ_i=1, both the risk and ∇_θR depend only on Σ_iλ_i, not on ||λ||. Appendix A.4 introduces −λ⊙∇R without justification. Indeed, the exact worst-case loss over an L2 parameter ball is also independent of λ, so sharpness does not select the claimed uniform mixture (1/p,…,1/p). This invalidates the principal theoretical evidence that ASGDRO balances invariant mechanisms.

Material conceptual gap: the manuscript assumes that single-feature mechanisms lie along linear parameter interpolations and inside a Euclidean neighborhood of the desired model, but neither the cited loss-basin observation nor Appendix A.2 proves this for neural networks. Parameter perturbations are not shown to correspond to removal of input features, so robustness to parameter-space sharpness does not imply robustness when an invariant visual cue is missing.

The formal setup has additional foundational problems. Invariance of E[Y|Z^I] for the complete feature set does not imply that every subset is invariant or individually sufficient, yet the argument treats singleton mechanisms as equally optimal. Definition 3 also ranges over all environments E, including unavailable test environments, whereas ASGDRO optimizes only E_tr; no generalization result connects these objectives. The empty subset and the representation of a varying-dimensional masked input are left undefined.

The theory does not match the evaluated algorithm: Eq. (3), Proposition 1, and Algorithm 1 use a separate adversarial perturbation for each environment, while Section 3.5 states that every non-toy experiment uses one perturbation computed from pooled empirical risk. There is no analysis or ablation showing that this approximation retains the claimed common-flat-minimum or SIL properties. Moreover, a small gradient norm alone does not characterize flatness—every differentiable stationary minimum has zero gradient regardless of Hessian curvature.

Only the synthetic H-CMNIST experiment directly tests performance after an invariant cue disappears, and its central gain has substantial variability over only three seeds. Standard subpopulation and domain-shift benchmarks support ASGDRO's predictive utility but do not establish that it learned multiple invariant cues. The selected Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and unquantified, while lower Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate curvature rather than feature diversity.

Algorithmic originality is limited because ASGDRO is largely a direct composition of GDRO and ASAM/SAM, while common-flat-minimum and balanced-feature motivations are already present in the cited literature. The paper lacks decisive controls on H-CMNIST such as feature/input dropout, masking or random erasing, relevant diverse-feature methods, and ablations of adaptive normalization, group weighting, radius, and shared versus per-environment perturbations.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing H-CMNIST sample counts and complete generation specifications, absent protocols for the MetaShift and Multi-NLI results shown only in Figure 7, and the lack of the efficiency or sensitivity analyses promised in the main text. Many comparisons use numbers reported by other papers rather than matched runs and search budgets. These are secondary to the theoretical issues but make the mechanism claims harder to verify.

strengths: The paper identifies an important failure mode: a predictor may learn one invariant cue yet fail when that cue is absent. The SIL framing and H-CMNIST construction make this motivation intuitive and relevant to robust computer vision.

ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and practically compatible with existing architectures. Combining group-robust weighting with adaptive sharpness-aware perturbations is potentially useful despite its incremental algorithmic nature.

The empirical evaluation is broad. ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44% to 69.17%, is best or competitive on four subpopulation benchmarks, leads the listed methods on five WILDS datasets, and improves training-domain-selected DPLCLIP DomainBed accuracy from 72.6% to 74.0%.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. It provides code, three-seed results, several hyperparameter grids, qualitative Grad-CAM analysis, and Hessian measurements.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result appears incorrect. Under Theorem 1's assumptions, Zθλ=sum_i λ_i=1 for every feasible λ, so the MSE risk and its actual gradient are independent of λ; if the singleton mechanisms are optimal for target 1, the gradient is zero. The proof introduces a λ-wise gradient scaling without justification, and the exact perturbation loss likewise cannot select the uniform mixture claimed by the theorem.

The SIL formalization relies on assumptions not implied by invariance. Joint invariance of ZI does not imply invariance or predictive sufficiency of every subset or singleton, contrary to the discussion in Section 3.2. Definition 3 also maximizes over all subsets, apparently including the empty set, and optimizes over all environments E although unseen environments are unavailable.

The claimed bridge from flatness to feature diversity is not established. A finite collection of invariant mechanisms is equated with every point in a parameter-space ball, and linear interpolation between mechanisms is assumed to preserve risk. Neither property generally holds for neural networks. Moreover, a small gradient norm alone does not imply a flat minimum, and Appendix A.5's assertion that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious features has no demonstrated basis.

The algorithm evaluated does not match the analyzed objective: Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use an environment-specific perturbation εe, whereas all substantive experiments use one perturbation computed from pooled empirical risk. Consequently, the theoretical claims about minimizing each environment's neighborhood risk do not directly apply to the reported method.

Direct evidence for SIL is limited to one synthetic benchmark with only three seeds and substantial variance for ASGDRO. The real-data experiments measure ordinary OOD or worst-group accuracy without controlled removal of individual invariant cues. Grad-CAM examples and lower Hessian eigenvalues do not establish that multiple independently sufficient invariant features were learned.

Comparison and reproducibility details weaken the empirical case. Many baselines are imported from prior papers rather than rerun under matched searches; WILDS training and model-selection details are largely absent; the original DomainBed results lack uncertainty estimates; and RxRx1 is reported as 32.2% in Table 3 but 30.5% in Figure 7. The promised efficiency and sensitivity analyses are also absent, while the method requires two forward/backward passes.

Overall, the empirical results are worthwhile, but the false or unsupported central theory and the lack of real-world evidence for the defining SIL claim are consequential rather than readily correctable presentation issues. They currently outweigh the paper's useful framing and benchmark gains.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful failure mode: a model may suppress spurious correlations yet depend on only one invariant cue, which can disappear at test time. H-CMNIST is a useful diagnostic that separates reliance on color, digit shape, and box position.

ASGDRO is simple and model-agnostic, combining adaptive sharpness perturbations with group-DRO weighting. The pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, three-seed results, and code link provide a reasonable implementation starting point.

The empirical scope is broad. ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy over GDRO (69.17% versus 61.44%), obtains competitive worst-group results on CMNIST, Waterbirds, CelebA, and CivilComments, and improves the five-dataset DomainBed average when added to DPLCLIP (74.0 versus 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO).
The authors include complementary Grad-CAM and Hessian analyses and explicitly acknowledge the approximately twofold training cost and the absence of a real-world SIL-specific benchmark.
weaknesses: Material: Theorem 1 is mathematically unsupported. With the stated linear model, Z=(1,...,1), theta_lambda=lambda, and sum(lambda)=1, the MSE and its parameter gradient depend only on sum(lambda), not on the distribution of its entries. The proof introduces the factor -lambda elementwise-multiplied by the gradient without derivation and turns Proposition 1's approximation into an equality. Indeed, the exact adversarial MSE is also independent of lambda, so the claimed unique uniform solution—and hence the central diversity guarantee—does not follow.

Material: The connection between weight-space flatness and robustness to missing input features is asserted rather than established. The equality between the worst risk over singleton mechanisms and the worst risk over an entire parameter ball is generally false; the ball contains arbitrary models, the mechanisms need not be linearly connected, and their distance is unknown. Moreover, a small first-order gradient at a minimum does not certify low curvature, and minimizing an outer maximum does not ensure every environment is flat.

Material: SIL itself is not well-defined at the claimed generality. The maximum over all subsets includes the empty set, while the appendix silently excludes it. The reduction to singleton subsets assumes every individual invariant feature is sufficient and that adding features cannot hurt—neither follows from Definition 1 and both fail for interacting features such as XOR. The definition also optimizes over all environments, including unseen ones.

Material: The method actually evaluated differs from the analyzed objective. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separate adversarial perturbation for every environment, whereas nearly all experiments use one perturbation computed from pooled empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel in that pooled perturbation, so the common-flatness argument does not transfer. No ablation compares these two variants or isolates adaptive sharpness from the group-DRO combination.

Material: Only synthetic H-CMNIST directly tests removal of an invariant cue, and its key result has high variability (69.17±6.19). Standard worst-group and domain-generalization gains demonstrate useful robustness but do not establish that diverse invariant mechanisms caused the gains. The selected Grad-CAM examples lack a quantitative diversity metric or sampling protocol, while raw Hessian eigenvalues are parameterization-sensitive and are reported without computation details or uncertainty.

Reporting/reproducibility: Table 3 reports ASGDRO RxRx1 accuracy as 32.2±0.2, whereas Figure 7 reports 30.5±0.1. Experimental details for the additional MetaShift and Multi-NLI results are absent, and runtime/memory measurements are not supplied despite the acknowledged extra pass. These are correctable issues, but they further weaken confidence in the evidence. Overall, the benchmark improvements are worthwhile, yet the invalid central theorem and missing evidence for the proposed SIL mechanism make the current balance favor rejection.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2bbh5772/call-5dac9af4956f44369930cda59747b1a7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} identifies an important failure mode: a predictor may rely on one invariant cue that is absent at test time. The proposed Sufficient Invariant Learning perspective is intuitive and potentially useful.
ASGDRO is simple, model-agnostic, and combines worst-group optimization with adaptive sharpness-aware perturbations. Its integration with DPLCLIP demonstrates practical composability.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering a controlled H-CMNIST diagnostic, four subpopulation-shift datasets, WILDS-style datasets, and five DomainBed datasets. ASGDRO obtains strong results, including 74.2 worst-group accuracy on CMNIST, 91.4 on Waterbirds, and a DPLCLIP DomainBed average of 74.0 versus 72.6 for ERM training and 72.9 for GDRO training.

H-CMNIST directly tests performance after removing the easy color cue, and the reported shape-only result improves from 61.44 for GDRO to 69.17 for ASGDRO. Grad-CAM and Hessian measurements provide useful, although not conclusive, complementary diagnostics.
The paper supplies pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, hardware information, three-seed results with error bars for major experiments, and a code URL, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not valid under its stated model. With Z=(1,...,1), θ_Iλ=λ, and sum_i λ_i=1, the stated MSE is R(θ)=0.5(Y-sum_i θ_i)^2, so ∇_θR=-(Y-1)1 is independent of λ; the exact L2-ball worst-case risk is also independent of λ. Appendix A.4 instead inserts -λ⊙∇R without justification, and therefore the claimed reduction to minimizing ||λ|| and the uniform-feature conclusion do not follow. This is a central technical error.

Several foundational steps are assumptions rather than established results. Joint invariance of Z^I does not imply that every singleton subset is invariant, predictive, or optimal; a multi-feature interaction can be predictive while every singleton is insufficient. Appendix A.2's monotonicity assumption does not prove that arbitrary feature subsets correspond to linear interpolations of singleton mechanisms, especially for nonlinear networks.

Proposition 1 gives the usual first-order SAM approximation, but a small gradient norm does not by itself imply flatness: every differentiable stationary minimum has zero gradient regardless of Hessian curvature. Consequently, it does not establish that ASGDRO finds common flat minima or that such minima imply robustness to missing features.

The analyzed objective and implemented algorithm differ materially. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use an environment-specific perturbation derived from each R_e, whereas all substantive experiments use one shared perturbation derived from aggregate empirical risk. No argument shows that this computational surrogate retains the claimed SIL guarantee.

Only the synthetic H-CMNIST experiment directly evaluates missing invariant cues. Standard subpopulation/domain-shift accuracy, lower Hessian eigenvalues, and larger Grad-CAM regions do not demonstrate that a model causally uses multiple independent invariant mechanisms. The qualitative saliency examples lack quantitative localization or feature-erasure validation.

In practice, ASGDRO largely resembles a shared ASAM perturbation followed by GDRO weighting. Comparisons against ASAM and GDRO separately indicate synergy, but the paper lacks controlled variants for environment-specific versus shared perturbations, non-adaptive SAM+GDRO, and matched extra-gradient computation; thus both the source of the gains and the algorithmic originality remain unclear.

Some comparisons use numbers reported by different papers and heterogeneous pretraining protocols rather than uniformly rerun baselines. Moreover, the key H-CMNIST shape-only result has substantial three-seed variability (69.17±6.19), and the method requires two forward/backward passes without a measured runtime or memory comparison. These limitations are secondary to the theoretical and evidentiary issues above, which make the current balance favor rejection despite the promising empirical results.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important failure mode: an invariant predictor may depend on only one valid cue and fail when that cue is occluded or missing. This is an intuitive and potentially useful extension of invariant-learning objectives. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6s40xw_6/call-0c8b273bd859474d82adc5b360de75e3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

H-CMNIST provides a controlled test of redundant invariant cues. When color is removed, ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy from GDRO's 61.44±1.03 to 69.17±6.19, suggesting that the proposed training rule can encourage use of the harder cue.

The empirical study is broad. ASGDRO obtains strong worst-group results on CMNIST, Waterbirds, and CelebA, improves the DPLCLIP DomainBed average from 72.6 to 74.0, and generally improves over GDRO on the reported WILDS tasks.

The method is simple, model-agnostic, and practically relevant where group or environment annotations exist. The paper also includes three-seed results, substantial implementation details, qualitative analyses, and a code link.
The motivation, figures, and high-level relationship among SIL, group robustness, and sharpness-aware optimization are generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: Material: Theorem 1 is mathematically incorrect. Under its own construction, θλ=λ, 1ᵀλ=1, and R(θλ)=0.5(Y−1)². Thus ∇θR=−(Y−1)1 is independent of λ; indeed, the exact inner maximum is 0.5(|Y−1|+ρ√p)², also independent of λ. The proof inserts an unexplained factor −λ⊙∇R and consequently cannot establish that ASGDRO selects λ=(1/p,…,1/p). This invalidates the main formal support for balanced use of invariant mechanisms.

Material: The SIL formulation is not justified by Definition 1. Conditional invariance given the full feature set need not remain true after marginalizing to a subset, and an invariant feature need not be individually predictive. Moreover, the maximum over all subsets formally includes the empty set. Appendix A.2 silently excludes it and adds the unproved assumption that additional observed features never hurt. Consequently, existence of optimal singleton mechanisms—and robustness to every singleton—does not follow from the stated setup.

Material: The bridge from parameter-space flatness to feature diversity is speculative. It assumes that singleton-feature solutions lie near the desired solution and along low-loss linear paths; the cited mode-connectivity observation does not imply this for different feature mechanisms. Maximizing loss over an entire parameter ball also does not specifically target those mechanisms.

Material: Proposition 1's first-order expansion does not prove convergence to flat minima: every differentiable stationary point has zero gradient, including arbitrarily sharp minima, and curvature appears only at second order. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, without a data model or derivation, that high-loss activated neurons encode spurious features; its update equation does not identify which neurons are spurious.

Material: The method analyzed is not the method used in most experiments. The theory and Algorithm 1 use a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, whereas the implementation uses one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. It also introduces ASAM's adaptive normalization, absent from the theorem. No ablation establishes that this practical approximation retains the claimed SIL property.

The controlled evidence for SIL is limited to one synthetic two-cue benchmark with three seeds and sizable variance. Standard shift benchmarks do not remove specific invariant cues, so their accuracy gains support generic robustness but not the claimed common-flat-minimum→diverse-features mechanism. Grad-CAM examples lack a quantitative metric or selection protocol, while the scale-dependent Hessian measurements lack error bars and sufficient computation details.

The algorithm is largely a direct composition of adaptive sharpness-aware minimization and GroupDRO. Given the invalid theoretical justification and limited mechanism-specific evidence, the remaining algorithmic originality is modest. Comparisons also mix newly tuned ASGDRO runs with literature-reported baselines, and runtime/memory overhead is not quantified despite requiring two forward/backward passes. These consequential issues outweigh the promising empirical results, so the balance favors rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful robustness problem: a predictor may fail when one of several nominally invariant cues becomes unavailable. The emphasis on redundant predictive evidence is intuitive and potentially useful.

ASGDRO is simple and model-agnostic, combining adaptive sharpness-aware optimization with group-robust weighting. It improves over GDRO in several reported settings—for example, H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy rises from 61.44% to 69.17%, and Waterbirds worst-group accuracy from 90.6% to 91.4%.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering a targeted synthetic benchmark, four subpopulation-shift datasets, WILDS tasks, and five DomainBed datasets. Reporting three-seed variability for many experiments and including groupwise Hessian and Grad-CAM analyses are useful efforts to examine behavior beyond average accuracy.

The manuscript is generally organized and supplies pseudocode, architectures, major hyperparameter ranges, and a public code link. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-umcmc8oe/call-68440773564a4211b27726e19c6ee56c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is incorrect. Under Theorem 1's own assumptions, Z=(1,...,1) and sum_i lambda_i=1 make the prediction, MSE risk, and its gradient independent of lambda; even the exact worst-case loss over an L2 ball is independent of lambda. The proof introduces -lambda elementwise-multiplied by the gradient without justification and then equates its norm to the product of the two norms, which is not generally valid. Consequently, the claimed preference for uniform feature weights—and hence the main theoretical support for learning diverse mechanisms—does not follow.

The SIL formalization is not sound as stated. Invariance of E[Y|Z^I] does not imply invariance or optimality for every subset of Z^I, contrary to Section 3.2. The maximization over all subsets also includes the empty set unless explicitly excluded, while requiring every singleton to predict well is much stronger than learning a merely sufficient collection of cues. Appendix A.2 obtains its singleton reduction only by assuming monotonic behavior rather than proving it, and it does not justify representing arbitrary nonlinear subset mechanisms by convex interpolation.

The bridge from flatness to SIL is unsupported. A finite set of hypothetical invariant mechanisms lying in a parameter ball would give only an inequality against the maximum over that ball, not the equality asserted in Section 3.3; moreover, parameter distance has no established correspondence to semantic feature diversity. Proposition 1 penalizes a first-order gradient norm, but every differentiable sharp minimum also has zero gradient, so this does not establish flatness or robustness to missing features. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, without derivation, that highly activated neurons in a high-loss environment encode spurious information.

The analyzed objective and implemented algorithm differ materially. Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 use a separate adversarial perturbation for each environment, whereas almost all experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Adaptive scaling also changes the perturbation geometry from the Euclidean ball used in the analysis. The stated theory therefore does not apply directly to the evaluated method.

Evidence for the paper's defining SIL claim is limited to one synthetic H-CMNIST construction. Ordinary OOD and worst-group accuracy cannot reveal whether a model learned multiple invariant cues rather than simply benefiting from generic regularization. The Grad-CAM examples are unquantified and selected, and larger attention regions do not establish use of distinct cues; raw Hessian eigenvalues are parameterization-sensitive and demonstrate neither cue diversity nor its causal role. No real-image intervention removes specified invariant parts such as beaks, tails, or feet.

ASGDRO is largely a direct composition of ASAM-style perturbation and GroupDRO. Although comparisons to ASAM and GDRO separately are included, there are no component ablations for adaptive versus standard SAM, shared versus per-group perturbations, or alternative sharpness-aware GroupDRO compositions. Thus neither the source of the gains nor the claimed algorithmic novelty is well isolated.

Several empirical gains are modest relative to the reported variability, many baseline numbers are imported from prior papers rather than rerun under one protocol, and only three seeds are used. The manuscript also promises efficiency and sensitivity analyses in the appendix, but does not provide them; WILDS training/model-selection details and H-CMNIST sample and validation details are incomplete. These reproducibility and presentation issues are secondary to the invalid central theory but further weaken the case.

strengths: The manuscript identifies an important robustness failure mode: removing spurious correlations does not ensure that a model learns redundant invariant cues that remain useful when one cue disappears. The SIL framing and motivating examples communicate this distinction clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-aunefcyf/call-177bb1b8598b4b7380cd6f776f4850e3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

ASGDRO is simple and model-agnostic, combining group-robust optimization with adaptive sharpness perturbations. The practical shared-perturbation implementation also avoids scaling the perturbation computation with the number of environments.

The evaluation is broad. ASGDRO improves H-CMNIST shape-only accuracy from 61.44% for GDRO to 69.17%, Waterbirds worst-group accuracy from 90.6% to 91.4%, and DPLCLIP's training-domain-selected DomainBed average from 72.6% to 74.0%. Results across subpopulation shifts, WILDS, and DomainBed suggest practical promise beyond one benchmark.

The paper provides pseudocode, many hyperparameter ranges, three-seed error bars for several experiments, a code link, Grad-CAM visualizations, and Hessian diagnostics. These are useful steps toward reproducibility and mechanism analysis.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Theorem 1 is false under its stated model. With Z=(1,...,1), theta_lambda=lambda, sum(lambda)=1, and R(theta)=0.5(Y-sum_i theta_i)^2, the exact adversarial risk is 0.5(|Y-1|+rho*sqrt(p))^2, independent of lambda. Thus the uniform lambda is not uniquely preferred. Appendix A.4 introduces a lambda-weighted gradient without justification, invalidating the central theoretical support for balanced invariant mechanisms.

Material technical issue: Proposition 1 is only a first-order SAM approximation and does not establish flatness. The gradient vanishes at any differentiable stationary minimum, whether sharp or flat, so minimizing its norm cannot by itself prove convergence to common flat minima. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes, without justification, that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious information; its update analysis does not identify which neurons are spurious.

Material theory-to-method gap: Equation (3) and the analysis use a separate worst-case perturbation for every environment, whereas nearly all experiments use one perturbation computed from average empirical risk. Environment gradients can cancel in this shared perturbation, so the stated common-flatness reasoning does not apply to the evaluated algorithm. No comparison of shared versus per-environment perturbations is reported.

Material evidence gap: H-CMNIST is the only experiment that directly removes one invariant cue. Ordinary OOD accuracy on the remaining datasets cannot distinguish SIL from generic regularization, and the H-CMNIST result uses only three seeds with substantial ASGDRO variability (69.17+/-6.19 versus 61.44+/-1.03 for GDRO). Grad-CAM is qualitative and non-causal, while raw Hessian eigenvalues are parameterization-dependent and are reported without uncertainty; neither establishes that multiple invariant mechanisms cause the gains on real images.

Material formulation issue: Definition 3 maximizes over all subsets, formally including the empty subset. The later reduction to singletons silently excludes it, assumes that adding features can never hurt, and claims without justification that arbitrary feature subsets are equivalent to linear interpolation of singleton parameter vectors. This is especially unsupported for nonlinear networks. The definition also depends on all environments, including unseen ones, with no theorem connecting optimization over training environments to the claimed missing-feature generalization.

Evidence and reproducibility limitations: Many comparison numbers are imported from prior papers rather than obtained in a controlled common pipeline. The ASGDRO WILDS setup is insufficiently specified, original ASGDRO DomainBed results lack uncertainty, statistical significance is not tested, and the acknowledged two-pass cost is not quantified. These issues are not individually decisive, but compound the central theory and attribution problems.

Presentation refinements are secondary: the manuscript is generally readable, but several conclusions use causal language stronger than the evidence, ASAM is inaccurately described as regularization-free, and notation alternates between all environments and training environments. The recommendation is driven by the technical and evidentiary issues above, not these editorial points.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and intuitive robustness failure: a model may learn an invariant cue yet fail when that particular cue is unavailable. Framing robustness in terms of redundant predictive cues is relevant to computer vision, especially under occlusion and cropping.

ASGDRO is a simple, model-agnostic combination of adaptive sharpness-aware optimization and group reweighting. It can be integrated into existing training pipelines, and the practical shared-perturbation implementation avoids a separate ascent step for every group.

The empirical scope is substantial. On the targeted H-CMNIST shape-only test, ASGDRO obtains 69.17±6.19 versus GDRO's 61.44±1.03; it also improves CelebA worst-group accuracy from 87.2 to 91.0 and raises the controlled DPLCLIP DomainBed average from 72.9 for DPLCLIP+GDRO to 74.0. These results suggest that the optimizer may be practically useful even independently of the SIL interpretation.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually coherent. It provides pseudocode, dataset and hyperparameter descriptions, three-seed error bars for many experiments, hardware information, a code URL, and an explicit discussion of the two-pass computational cost and synthetic-only SIL benchmark limitation. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-253you1u/call-4bd46dc9f3684fa4959fe868ae5be4a2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The foundational argument is incorrect. Definition 1 establishes invariance only for the complete feature set Z^I, but Section 3.2 asserts that it therefore holds for every subset and that a classifier using any subset can be optimal. Conditional invariance is not preserved under marginalizing features, and invariant features can be predictive only jointly—for example, an XOR mechanism. Thus the assumed singleton invariant mechanisms need not exist.

Definition 3 is not technically well-posed as stated. It optimizes over all environments E, including unseen ones, and all subsets of Z^I, apparently including the empty set, without defining how one classifier accepts different subsets or specifying a missingness/intervention distribution. Even if the empty set is excluded, the appendix's reduction to singleton subsets assumes rather than proves that every individual cue is sufficient and that adding observed features monotonically reduces a fixed classifier's expected loss.

Theorem 1 is false under its own assumptions. With Z=(1,...,1) and sum_i lambda_i=1, every lambda produces the same linear prediction; consequently both the MSE gradient and the exact isotropic L2-perturbed risk are independent of lambda. The proof obtains a preference for uniform lambda by inserting lambda elementwise into the gradient and deriving a factor ||lambda||, but that operation does not follow from Equation 3. Therefore the principal theoretical support for balanced use of invariant mechanisms fails.

The bridge from flatness to SIL is otherwise unsupported. A Euclidean parameter ball is not the set of models using alternative invariant cues, so replacing the maximum over invariant mechanisms by a maximum over arbitrary perturbations is unjustified; nonlinear parameter interpolation is also not equivalent to combining features. Moreover, first-order gradient norm cannot distinguish sharp and flat stationary minima, where every gradient is zero. Appendix A.5 likewise assumes without justification that high-risk activated neurons encode spurious features.

The implemented algorithm differs materially from the analyzed objective: almost all experiments use one perturbation computed from average risk rather than separate worst-case perturbations for each environment. Opposing group gradients can cancel, so this is not an approximation with an established relation to the claimed common-flat-minimum objective.

Evidence for the central SIL claim is limited to one two-cue synthetic benchmark. Its three-seed shape-only result has high variance, while the standard subpopulation, WILDS, and DomainBed evaluations test general robustness rather than removal of invariant cues. Grad-CAM examples have no selection protocol or quantitative diversity measure, and broader attention maps do not prove use of multiple causal cues. Hessian eigenvalues support only flatter parameter-space solutions—not feature diversity or robustness to missing cues—and lack uncertainty and scale-invariant analysis.

The empirical gains do not fully establish originality or isolate the cause. Many baseline values are imported, the authors' WILDS and original DomainBed configurations are incompletely specified, and there are no component ablations for adaptive normalization, group reweighting, or shared versus per-environment perturbations. Since the practical method is essentially ASAM/SAM combined with GDRO, these omissions make it difficult to separate a novel SIL mechanism from generic sharpness regularization. The promising benchmark gains are worthwhile, but the invalid central theorem and missing evidence for the claimed mechanism determine the weak-reject recommendation.
